segments.header: ORAL ARGUMENT OF KEVIN JOEL PAGE ON BEHALF OF THE PETITIONER
ORAL ARGUMENT OF ERIC J. FEIGIN ON BEHALF OF THE RESPONDENT, IN SUPPORT OF VACATUR
ORAL ARGUMENT OF ANTHONY J. DICK, COURT-APPOINTED AMICUS CURIAE
REBUTTAL ARGUMENT OF KEVIN JOEL PAGE ON BEHALF OF THE PETITIONER

turns.x: We will hear argument this morning in Case Number 25-5343, Beaird versus United States. Mr. Page.

Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: For two reasons, the courts below erred in deferring to the commentary when interpreting Guideline 2K2.1. First, the proper rule for deference to guideline commentary is no deference. Nothing in the text of the Sentencing Reform Act suggests that courts must ever defer to commentary when interpreting a guideline, let alone defer on the -- according to the extreme rule of Stinson. That alone should resolve the question presented given the baseline expectation that courts independently determine the meaning of legal provisions. That expectation dates back to Marbury, and it should be especially hard to displace in the criminal setting, where respect for liberty demands that we turn square corners. In fact, the Sentencing Reform Act is affirmatively incompatible with any deference regime. Section -- Section 3553(a)(4) requires that the Commission set forth the range of imprisonment in the guidelines, not elsewhere. And Sections 994 and 995 of Title 28 attach detailed procedural requirements to the amendment of guidelines, which requirements do not apply to guideline commentary. Why would Congress bother to require detailed notice, public comment, 180 days of congressional review, and the approval of four voting commissioners every time the -- the Commission amends a guideline if the Commission could simply bind the courts to a new interpretation of the guideline without going through all of this simply by amending the commentary? The second reason the courts below erred in affording Stinson deference is that if the Sentencing Reform Act leaves room for deference, the proper predicate is genuine ambiguity of the kind that survives every tool of construction, not the mere absence of plain or flat inconsistency, as Stinson suggests. The rule applied below, which requires courts to construe guidelines in ways that they think are wrong, certainly can't be found in the SRA's text, and it is not consistent with the judicial role. I am pleased to take the Court's questions.
What do you do with Kisor?

The significant fact of Kisor is that it weakens the force of stare decisis in -- in -- because it -- it weakens Seminole Rock, and so, for that reason, the Court should return to first principles and reconsider the terms of the statute. My first-line position, my primary rule that I suggest the Court ought to follow is that it should simply review the text of the Sentencing Reform Act and ought to, therefore, conclude that no deference is appropriate. However, if it believes that -- that Kisor sets forth the appropriate rule for agencies, at least the rule here ought to be as favorable to judicial resolution of legal provisions as was Kisor.

Of course, after Booker, the guidelines are advisory. And I'm not sure why we should invite the lower courts to engage in somewhat it strikes me as an academic exercise of interpreting. Why don't they just look at what the Commission meant in the guidelines and move on to the 3553(a) factors? I just think -- I'm not quite sure that, you know, Stinson is not a more workable regime.

The -- the simple answer is it is not the question -- it is not the process that the Sentencing Reform Act calls for. It is not what the statute calls for. The statute indicates that the courts are to find the sentencing range in the guidelines themselves. It distinguishes between guidelines and commentary in terms of how they are created, and those are different categories of enactments, and, therefore, the guidelines must be determined independently.

While they're different categories of enactments, I think what concerns me about your arguments is that you're suggesting that they are separable in some way which is really not the way in which the guidelines were devised. And I think we sort of have a -- a fundamental misunderstanding of how the manual works because the guidelines and commentary are actually inextricably linked. And what I mean by that is that sentencing judges use the Guidelines Manual to do what is essentially a calculation. It's kind of like math, that the guidelines themselves have certain components to them, and the commentary tells you how those pieces fit together, how you are supposed to take them into account. When you are a judge, you're using both to reach the right answer under the guidelines, and there is a right answer as to what the guideline range is. And so what concerns me about your way of framing this is you suggest that the court can somehow look at the guidelines, not take into account the commentary, not defer to it, not use it, and yet still have an accurate guideline calculation, which is really not how the system is designed. So can you -- can you respond to that?

Of course. Stinson presumes that the guidelines have a freestanding meaning. Stinson says that the guidelines mean one thing, and if the Commission -- and if the commentary is plainly inconsistent with them, we are to disregard them. So the assumption that the Commission has always been using or should have always been using -- and it has -- is that you can determine a meaning from the guidelines alone and resort to the commentary --

But it's a very, very narrow category. I mean, as Stinson understood it, the guidelines have a meaning, obviously, but if the commentary says something that is totally inconsistent, then you have a problem. But, if it's not inconsistent, then I don't take Stinson to say you shouldn't be reading them in coordination, in conjunction. The problem arises just when the judge doesn't know what to do because the guidelines say one thing and the commentary says something totally different. What you're suggesting is that even when the two can be reconciled, the commentary can be disregarded and we don't have to pay attention to it in understanding the guidelines, and -- and -- and that, I don't think, is how the guidelines are designed.

So it -- whether or not it is how the guidelines are designed, it is how the statute is designed. The statute says that the sentencing range is set forth in the guidelines. The only mention of commentary in the Sentencing Reform Act is in 3553(b)(1), which says that the commentary may be of use in determining when it is appropriate or not appropriate to depart. So, if we look at the text of the statute alone and we look at the cues from the structure of 994, specifically the heightened procedural requirements of guidelines in preference to commentary, we can tell -- we can see a congressional intent that the sentencing range should be determined by --
I'm sorry. Keep going.
Well --
No, of course.

Stinson looked at all that 30 years ago and came to the conclusion that the commentary was binding, controlling, force of law, and went through this whole exercise. And since then, as the Chief Justice said, the one major change in the sentencing realm is that those guidelines are no longer, as a whole, binding. They're advisory. So I guess Stinson plus Booker together suggests that we've already been down this road, it's been that way for 30 years. 1B1.7 of the -- of the guidelines itself says the commentary has the force of law. The commentary to that says that. So, given all that, why are we reinventing the wheel when Stinson did this 30 -- 30-some years ago?

Well, first of all, I don't think that we can say that -- that Congress or any other objective observer can -- could confidently say that Stinson sets forth the rule that governs the relationship between -- between commentary and guidelines at least since Kisor, right? We -- we -- we -- the -- the apple cart has already been upset, and now we are just trying to -- please.
Why?
I'm sorry?
Counsel --
Yeah.
-- why? Why has Kisor upset the apple cart?
Well --

We reference -- we reference Seminole Rock as an imprecise analogy, but we relied on the guideline, 1B1.7, which tells us that the commentary should -- should be followed. And we relied on Williams. And we relied on the structure of the guidelines system and said that -- and we announced the level of deference. Why did Kisor upset that?
Well, first, we can answer the question empirically and see that in half of the circuits that under the --

Yeah, half the circuits may have gotten it wrong, but what does that have to do with anything? The other half have said it has no application. Other than that uncertainty, the courts have been pretty clear of what to do, right? Kisor's the only thing that introduced uncertainty.

Well, I mean, I think that's a bit post ergo, post hoc. Since Kisor, there has been more uncertainty. But, as Judge Bibas explained in Nasir, Kisor sort of awakened us from a doctrinal slumber in which we -- we moved from a position where, essentially, the -- the -- the commentary was --

Let me ask you how this operates, and -- and let's take this -- this -- this -- this guideline, okay? The -- the guideline says the application -- let's look at the guideline. It defines it as a semi-automatic firearm that is capable of accepting a large capacity magazine, okay? That's the guideline. That gives you the enhancement under the guideline. The application note says -- makes it clear that this refers only to a firearm that "at the time of the offense either had attached to it or had in close proximity a large capacity magazine." If I read the guideline just as a guideline and it says you apply the enhancement to a semi-automatic firearm that is capable of accepting a large capacity magazine, I look at the structure of the gun, and if it's capable of it, I don't care where the magazine is or what size the magazine is because the words of the guideline say capable. So, if I decide that, wouldn't I be more punitive if I decided that large capacity firearm meant any firearm that was built to hold a large magazine?

In this particular case, no. And the reason we take that position or the reason we believe that is that to say that -- that a gun is capable of accepting a large capacity magazine might mean that it is physically capable if a large capacity magazine were present, or it might mean that --

But that's not what the guideline says. All I'm suggesting to you is it's only by reading the application note do I know that the magazine has to be attached to it or have -- or be in close proximity. It's only the application note that tells us.

My -- respectfully, I disagree that that comes only from the application note, and the reason is that capable -- there is an ambiguity in what "capable of accepting a large capacity magazine" means. It might mean capable --
But I'm -- I'm a literalist. Capable to me means you can do it.
What --
You can -- you can give me any alternative you want, but if -- without the application note, you're creating a sea of confusion for district court judges to fill in the blanks --
-- when the application note makes it very clear what it means.
So the application note does have some clarifying function, but anything that the Commission could do to clarify in the text of a commentary, it could do to --
So you're suggesting your rule is more workable than Stinson?
Yes, I do believe it is.

All right. So now we have ambiguity as to what "capable" means. We have ambiguity as to how large the magazine has to be. And that's less workable following the application note than your system of letting every district court judge have to define these terms anew --
So --
-- and decide what they mean anew. That's more workable for you?

Well, so in -- a couple of things will assist in containing any disuniformity in the precedent. The first is that the courts can still use the -- the commentary as an interpretive aid as they would under Skidmore, which will -- means that it will still have a sort of anchoring effect and contain any disruption to the system. The second thing is that the -- the -- the Sentencing Commission is uniquely created to respond to disruptions to its precedent and to disuniformity in its precedent, and Congress's intended way of dealing with disuniformity in the precedent is for them to meet every year and amend the text of the guidelines.
Do you think, Mr. --
It's called -- sorry, please.
Do you think, Mr. Page, that the Commission needs to defer to the Commission's policy statements, as Williams indicated?
The courts or the Commission?
I'm sorry, that the -- that the -- that the courts need to defer.
Interpretive policy statements I do not believe carry binding deference any more than commentary. And that comes from, first of all, 3553(a)(4), which says that the sentencing range is --
So that's -- that's the opposite of what we said in Williams. So you're asking us not only to overthrow Stinson but to overthrow Williams as well?

Well, no. I think that in Williams, the Court was dealing with a -- was not dealing with an interpretive policy statement that amended another guideline. It was dealing with a policy statement that limited when we could depart -- when the court could depart from the guidelines, and that's all that was at issue in -- in Williams.
Not -- you don't take Williams to be talking about policy statements generally?

I don't take it to be talking about interpretive policy statements. I take it to be saying that policy statements can limit -- and -- and this was the clear impact of 3553(b)(1) in the pre-Booker era -- when a court could depart and that they were effectively mandatory in that realm before Booker. And there simply isn't -- there wasn't a guideline that the policy statement was interpreting. So it's very difficult to see it as an interpretive policy concerning that.
Mr. Page, on stare decisis, it seems to me we -- we first have to acknowledge that the circuits are currently badly split and somebody is going to be -- existing law below is going to be rejected.
I -- I think that's clear.
That's yes. And second, we'd have to decide that interpretive principles are entitled to stare decisis effect, something about which judges on this Court have -- have opined different ways.
Correct. That's the second issue presented.

And then the next thing we'd have to look at is the quality of reasoning. And Stinson relied on silence being enough to be an implicit delegation of -- of interpretive authority and that their ambiguity is the appropriate trigger, both of which we've since rejected in Loper Bright.
Indeed. And it would have to require on silence to -- to create deference in the criminal setting particularly.

Yeah. And you'd have to say that 994, which says, right, not even commentary but interpretive guidance is -- plus 3553, which says to courts consider, is somehow an express delegation of interpretive authority, exclusive interpretive authority in the Commission.
It seems, if that's a -- an express delegation, you will find express delegations of interpretive authority all over the place.
And then you'd have to say, well, it's consistent somehow with Booker even though Booker -- the whole point of Booker is that everything's supposed to be advisory in this area, not mandatory.
I think Your Honor is right.
And then -- and then, on terms of reliance, I mean, does any criminal in the country rely on the commentary of the guidelines when deciding whether to commit a crime?
No. I think the only reliance interests are those of the Commission, and they can be easily dealt with by moving text from -- to the commentary.
Thank you.
Can I just --

Thank you, counsel. You -- you argue that Loper Bright undermined Stinson. And Loper Bright concerned executive agencies interpreting statutes instead of -- instead of courts interpreting them. And I just don't see what Stinson, which involves an agency in the judicial branch and issues non-binding advice, really has much to do with Loper Bright at all.

Well, Loper Bright, first of all, it indicated that -- that statutes have a -- a single best meaning rather than a range of permissible meanings, and it rejected the idea of an implied delegation of interpretive authority. Perhaps the Court could distinguish agencies and statutes on that ground and say that for some reason, those principles do not apply to regulations or agency -- agencies. But, if it were to distinguish an agency, it oughtn't distinguish the Sentencing Commission, which deals with particularly the sentencing realm, where there is a -- ought to be a strong expectation that judges will resolve those questions that determine the defendant's fate rather than defer to another actor.
Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

You began by saying the -- the rule in a case like this should be no deference. Now the ultimate question here, as Justice Sotomayor was discussing, includes the term "large capacity magazine." So let's say you are a district judge and you are not to defer to the commentary of the Sentencing Commission as to what constitutes a large capacity magazine. How do you go about deciding what that means?
You use the -- the text and the structure of the guidelines, just as you use the text and structure of the other --
Yeah, concretely. Concretely. You have the term "large." What is large?

"Large" means large for a semi-automatic firearm. So whatever that is, it isn't 17, which is the average. And we look at (a)(2), which provides -- excuse me, (a)(3), which provides the same adjustment for a large capacity magazine that is provided for a bomb, a -- or a machine gun or a sawed-off shotgun. And we ask, is the average gun really merit the same kind of adjustment? Did the Commission mean that?

So the -- your -- your -- your methodology would be to examine all semi-automatic weapons and see what is the average, and so whatever is above the average, that would be the -- the large capacity magazine?
So I don't know that -- that something that's just above the median would necessarily qualify, and so there would -- there could be potentially edge cases. And -- and -- and -- and --
But I just don't see how this could possibly work without some degree of deference to what is essentially a policy call by the Sentencing Commission.
The -- the Sentencing Commission is free to make that policy call. It needs to do that in the text because that is where the -- the Sentencing Reform Act told them to resolve questions of that sort.
It has to be in a guideline?
It has to be in a guideline.
It can't be in a policy statement?

No. In my view, it -- it cannot. A policy statement is not -- does not have the binding authority to determine the guideline range. And the reason that we know that is because 3553(a)(4) says that the range is set forth in the guidelines and because -- because they are distinguished in 3553(b)(1) and because of the different procedure.
Do they go through notice and comment?
Typically, yes. They don't have to.
Does commentary typically go through notice and comment?
Typically, yes.
What was your answer to the question whether we have to overrule Williams? Yes or no?

I -- the -- the holding of Williams itself, no, I don't believe you do because the -- the -- Williams concerned a -- a -- did not concern an interpretive policy statement of any kind, so we don't have to -- we also don't have a policy statement here. We have commentary. And those are distinguished in 3553(b)(1) and throughout the Guideline Manual.

One might wonder what practical difference the issue here makes. First of all, the guidelines are now simply advisory. Second, the district court here stated that "even if the guideline range was not calculated or applied correctly," it would have imposed the same sentence regardless of the applicable guideline range.
So --
So why does this matter for your client?

-- the Fifth Circuit has consistently -- well, not consistently, but it has often said that it does not take such statements at face value, that it undertakes a separate harmless error analysis in that circumstance. And that is a recognition of the fact that there are courts that say this in literally every sentencing case.

So it doesn't believe these judges? You think -- he says -- they think these judges are lying when the judge says, look, I've gone through this whole guidelines calculation, but it doesn't really matter, I'd impose the same sentence even if the guidelines didn't come into play at all? That's a lie?

I don't know that it thinks that they are lying, but I think that it may think that they have included a boilerplate statement in -- and that it may -- they may have over- -- underestimated the impact of the guidelines on their own thinking.
Justice Sotomayor?

I'm not sure I understood your answer to Justice Alito about Williams. Williams said that policy statements had to be followed, correct? That's the same thing Stinson says, that commentary has to be followed.
It -- it said that in a particular context.
The context there was a policy statement that said that district courts couldn't do certain things, correct?
That it -- that they could not depart. And that came from 3553(b)(1) because it had -- and it had an express statutory basis.
So a policy statement that operates the way this does, which talks about what something means, would have to -- we would have to overrule that part of Williams's holding, correct?
I don't think that Williams expressly addressed that.
Williams said we had -- district courts had to follow policy statements in all circumstances to calculate the guidelines. That's how I read Williams's holding.
That question is not before you --
I know it's not, counsel. Assume it were. Would you overrule that part of Williams?
Insofar as it affects this case, then that part of Williams --

I didn't say I took it out of this case. If the holding in Williams, as I read it, was that district courts are required to apply the policy statements in calculating guidelines, would that holding be overruled or more limited by your view under --
If -- if the Court were of the opinion that that is the holding of Williams, it would be limited. However, either --
What would be limited?
The holding of Williams would be limited to the --
That some part of -- of Williams would have to be overruled, correct?
I -- in my view, Williams does not speak to --
All right.
-- the calculation of guidelines.
We'll fight about that after. We can go -- both go look back at it.
Justice Kagan?
So, again, on policy statements, Mr. Page, Congress specifically authorizes the Commission to issue policy statements. Is that correct?
It does.
So we're not talking about implied or implicit delegations. We're talking about an express delegation to the Commission?

In my view, we are talking about an implied delegation because we are talking about an implied delegation to create binding policy statements, whereas what -- what the -- what is expressly delegated is the -- the ability to create policy statements of some kind.
Okay. Well, we'll get to whether it's binding or not. But there's an express delegation authorizing the creation of policy statements, correct? I mean, you have to say yes to that.
Obviously, yes.

And -- and -- and what a policy statement is is defined very broadly. The Commission can issue general policy statements -- and I'm -- I'm quoting here -- "regarding application of the guidelines or any other aspect of sentencing or sentencing implementation." That's what the Commission can do, correct?
That is the statutory text, yes.
So -- so suppose that all the commentary in the sentencing manual was just relabeled as policy statements, that there's an express authorization to issue those, correct?
If -- the Court -- the Sentencing Commission could redefine commentary through the appropriate procedures as policy statement or as guideline if it wished to change the legal effect of them.

Well, I mean, what I'm getting at is that the -- the policy statements have a very broad definition encompassing everything that's found in the commentary. So, if the Commission just took all the commentary and relabeled it as policy statements, Congress would have expressly authorized it. I would think that the -- the result of that, the implication of that is that, of course, Congress meant for courts to follow it in the same way that courts have to follow -- you know, had to follow guidelines.

Well, so there are policy statements that Congress has specifically stated that courts must follow. Those are in 3582(c)(1), (c)(2), 3583(d)(3), right? There is no general statement that courts must follow policy statements.

No, there's not a general statement, but there's an express authorization to create these policy statements. Do you think that -- that Congress meant that the Commission should create these policy statements and then people could take them for whatever they were worth, that that's all it was?

Yes. I mean, to the extent that a policy statement interprets a guideline, yes. That is -- that is precisely what Congress intended if -- if it authorized interpretive policy statements at all. Now one reason that we know this is not a policy statement is, number one, they are expressly distinguished from commentary in 3553(b)(1), and, second, because the Commission has consistently distinguished between policy statements and commentary.
Thank you.
Justice Gorsuch?
994 says they may issue policy statements silent as to commentary.
Correct.
So, first, we'd have to somehow conflate those two.
Correct, and in spite of 3553(b)(1).
And then 3553(a) generally says, you consider the commentary and the guidelines -- sorry, the -- the guidelines and the policy statements.
Correct.
If we found that were enough to commit to the Commission the power to issue binding, on courts, binding interpretations, what would be left of Loper Bright?
Well, I mean --
Because doesn't every agency have the power to issue -- most agencies have the power to issue interpretive rules?
I think you would have to find that there is a --
And guidance documents? That's all within their power. And -- and, here, all Congress has said is consider them.
Correct.
It would be a pretty --
I will -- I will say that --
-- pretty big hole in Loper Bright.

Well, I -- I will say that I don't -- I'm not sure that the -- the force of the precedent at issue here would necessarily -- necessarily has to extend beyond the sentencing context. There is -- well, it's even under --
Oh, you don't think -- you don't think the federal government's other agencies will come in here and say, we've got similar language?
I think they would say it.
Okay.
Right.
And then -- and then doesn't Congress know how to tell us when it wants us to follow policy statements?
It -- it does.
I'm looking at 3553(e), for example, just one example, that in those circumstances, the sentence shall be imposed in accordance with the guidelines and policy statements. There it is.
Correct, correct, in several places throughout the code.
Several places. So, if -- if -- if we're looking at contextual clues, we would say this is very different than those?
Indeed.
Okay. And then Williams, I thought that to be about 3553(b), which is no longer enforceable.
Correct.
Yeah. Thanks.
Justice Kavanaugh?

On Justice Kagan's question about policy statements versus the commentary, I'd be interested in what you do with 994(a)(2), where it says policy statements are regarding application of the guidelines and the commentary is typically labeled application notes. The same word, "application," would suggest that that commentary is a policy statement because policy statements are regarding application of the guidelines. Just curious on your thoughts on that.

Well, so two points about that. The first is that I think when it refers to a general policy statement concerning application of the guideline, it's talking about things like 1B1.10, 1B1.13 or 6A3, the standard of proof, that address questions about how to apply the guidelines without determining -- that -- that -- but they're not talking about the category of offender or the category of offense. Those are to be determined by the guidelines, and we know that from 3553(a)(4). Now, whether the -- the Commission intended to say that policy statements -- that commentary was a policy statement because it used the term "application notes," to me, that doesn't quite follow because they also labeled it commentary, and the statute itself indicates in 3553(b)(1) that those are specific. They also attach commentary to policy statements, which would be strange -- a strange thing to do if they were the same.

Then, on Congress's understanding, I guess, of -- of the process, 1B1.7, as I mentioned earlier, since 1987 has specifically said commentary is to be construed to have the same force as policy statements. What do you do with that?
So --

Congress has never -- even though Congress has actually, as you know, overturned certain commentary, Congress has never reacted to 1B1.7 or the commentary to 1B1.7, which has been in place since 1987 on this.
Congress does not legislate by acquiescence. It does not legislate merely because --

But it gets the guideline amendments each year, and the House and Senate Judiciary Committees get that, and I think its understanding would -- everyone's understanding since 1987 was confirmed by Williams and Stinson, was that those policies -- those commentary is -- has the force of policy statements.
Well, so I -- I -- I do not agree that the Commission giving Congress notice that it wants to -- to promulgate a species of enactment --

It's a fair point. That's a -- that's a fair point. On -- on -- just quickly on Williams and Stinson, I mean, Williams -- Stinson says the principle that the Guidelines Manual is binding on federal courts applies as well to policy statements, and Williams, we said, where a policy statement prohibits a district court from taking a specified action, the statement is an authoritative guide to the meaning of the applicable guideline. And then the next page, 43, Stinson says, our holding in Williams dealing with policy statements applies with equal force to the commentary before us here. I mean, I think you have a little bit of a problem with Williams if you're -- you're fighting pretty hard on that.

Well, the -- the -- the strange -- I mean, that language in Williams is a little bit strange for its context. It's talking -- it says the meaning of the guidelines, but it's not really talking about the meaning of any individual provision. I think what it meant to say, what it was saying when it said the meaning of the guidelines is the outcome dictated by the Guidelines Manual. And it was speaking about that in the context -- in a very different sentencing system, where the Guidelines Manual dictated a particular result and it wasn't talking about a provision that -- that changes the meaning of a guideline.

Last one. Justice Gorsuch's good questions about Loper Bright and what's binding. I mean, isn't Booker a game-changer on that in the sense that whatever you come up with as a district judge in terms of following the guidelines, following the policy statements, following the commentary, is then only advisory and the district judge then can determine whether to vary up or down. And it seems to me that really distinguishes this from kind of the whole executive branch situation at least potentially. I want to get your reaction to that possibility that Booker mitigates the concern there.

So Booker doesn't change the fact that the -- that the Sentencing Reform Act commits a piece of legal text, requires a court to -- and -- and requires a court to interpret it. And the baseline expectation is that when that occurs, that legal issue will be decided by an Article III judge. It's no different, say, than a Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure which said --
Then it's not going to be binding at all, the judge, I mean on anyone, right?
Well, I mean, it's binding on --
Given Booker?

It's not binding as to the ultimate sentence. It still has determinate legal consequences. It states what -- what courts must do to explain the sentence. It affects the standard. It is reviewed de novo by a court, and a defendant can -- and a court can be reversed for failing --
Thank you.
-- to get it right. Thank you.
Justice Barrett?

So the Sentencing Reform Act tells district courts that they have to follow the guidelines, putting aside Booker here, but, you know, they do have to -- and we've said to district courts that you have to accurately calculate the guidelines range even though you can depart from it. What if the Sentencing Commission adopted a guideline saying that the commentary authoritarily -- authoritatively interprets our guidelines?
So --

Stronger than 1 -- 1B17 because that's a little bit equivocal. It may give background. It could be reversible error. So, if -- if that guideline were amended to say something very definitive, what would your response be?

If the Commission did that through notice and comment, it called that new guideline a guideline, it would be within its power to do, it would be strange because there is a lot of things in the commentary that do not directly interpret a guideline, so it wouldn't be clear how to make binding force of it. But -- but, if Your Honor's point is that the -- the -- that the Commission can interpret its own guidelines through a guideline, of course, it can.
It just seems then that this is all about nomenclature.
Right. So it is a label chosen by the Sentencing Commission, and that label has a consequence of -- according to the Sentencing Reform Act. So --

Well, why is it so important to you if, as a practical matter, the commentary goes through the same process as the guidelines do, goes through notice and comment, Justice Alito asked you about this, and then goes to Congress, just like the guidelines. Then what is the practical difference?

So the -- the practical -- I mean, the difference -- the important difference is that these are different categories of enactments that are set forth in the Sentencing Reform Act. We could treat all commentary as binding if it goes through notice and comment, and perhaps that would be -- achieve Congress's goals maybe, but that's not the way that Congress chose to -- to -- to create its goals. And the -- to achieve its goals. What it chose to do was to create three different categories of enactments and that the -- and that only guidelines would determine the sentencing range.

Why do you think the Commission -- is it your sense that the Commission, by calling this commentary, is somehow pulling a fast one, getting things into the commentary that it might not be able to put into the guideline itself?

So the Commission has been staffed by conscientious public servants who are conscientious of their role, and they have not attempted in general to -- to -- to circumvent anything. But the -- the -- the more important point is that this speaks to congressional intent. It speaks to congressional intent that it would not have undermined the procedural requirements that it stated in 994 by permitting the -- the Sentencing Commission to do that or even leaving that opportunity on the table.

Okay. One last question about Stinson and stare decisis. I'm thinking about probation offices. You know, they're the ones that calculate in the PSR, and, presumably, the commentary application notes are very helpful to probation officers. So is the idea that if Stinson goes, probation officers are then interpreting the guidelines and can't treat the -- you know, de novo themselves and can't treat the application notes as -- you know, or give deference to the application notes?

So, I mean, the application notes will still be available as -- as an interpretive aid. It's not that anybody has to cover their eyes when they are interpreting a guideline. But I would say that anybody who is trying to reach a correct result about the meaning of the guideline must confine themselves to the guideline when determining what is dispositive in deciding the meaning of that.
Thank you.

It will resolve the -- one concern about dis-uniformity in the precedent because the -- the policy statements and the commentary will be available to resolve cases of grave ambiguity. It will resolve the -- any concerns the Court may have about stare decisis because the Court wouldn't be doing anything in the sentencing context to move from Stinson to Kisor that it didn't do in the agency context to go from Seminole Rock to Kisor. And if Williams pertains, it -- and I don't think a move to Kisor would undermine Williams in any way -- because if Williams pertains to the interpretation of guidelines through policy statements, then there isn't any reason that Kisor wouldn't apply to that as well. As to the concern about whether or not moving to Kisor would open the floodgates to a number of resentencings, first of all, there are only a few cases of -- of tension between commentary and -- and the text of a guideline that have actually been litigated in this case, so I don't think that we can say that -- that every defendant will have an opportunity to challenge their guideline -- that it has arisen in 2(b)(1.1) , it has arisen in -- in this case and it has arisen in 4(b)(1.2) and there has been one issue about the -- the issue of what a dangerous weapon is, but there has not been a floodgate of people asserting, even in a world where Kisor might be thought to apply to the guidelines, that their guideline calculations are infirm. And we can take, I think my friend at his word and at his analysis that -- that Kisor would limit the amount of resentencing litigation that would happen or at least the amount of resentencings as well. Thank you.
